entry: Metropolis in [[Assam]], [[India]]. Guwahati is the largest city in the state and the largest metropolis in [[Northeast India|northeastern India]], known as the "gateway to North East India". It lies on the south bank of the [[Brahmaputra River]], between the river and the foothills of the Shillong plateau. Dispur, the state capital, lies within the Guwahati circuit city region. Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport is the 10th busiest in India. The ancient cities of Pragjyotishpura and Durjaya were capitals of the ancient state of Kamarupa. Many Hindu temples, including the Kamakhya Temple, give the city the title "The City of Temples". The name derives from the Assamese word "Guwa", itself from the [[Sanskrit]] "guvāka" meaning areca nut. The Guwahati Municipal Corporation administers 523 square kilometers (202 sq mi).

English Catholic conspirator in the [[Gunpowder Plot]]. Born in [[York]], Fawkes converted to Catholicism and fought for Catholic Spain in the [[Eighty Years' War]]. He joined Robert Catesby's plot to assassinate King James I, and was put in charge of gunpowder stockpiled beneath the [[House of Lords]]. Found guarding the explosives on 5 November 1605, he was tortured and confessed. Sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered, he died when his neck broke at the hanging; some sources say he jumped deliberately. The plot's failure is commemorated in the UK as Guy Fawkes Night, when his effigy is burned on a bonfire.

American restaurateur, author and television presenter. Fieri co-owned three now-defunct restaurants in California and licenses his name to restaurants in cities worldwide. He is known for hosting television series on the Food Network. In 2010, [[The New York Times]] reported that he had become the "face of the network", bringing "an element of rowdy, mass-market culture" to American food television. Born in [[Columbus, Ohio]], he graduated from the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, with a degree in hotel management. His first New York City restaurant, Guy's American Kitchen and Bar, opened in 2012 and closed at the end of 2017.

French author, celebrated as a master of the [[Short story|short story]]. Maupassant was a protégé of [[Gustave Flaubert]], and his stories are characterized by economy of style and efficient, seemingly effortless endings. He wrote 300 short stories, six novels, three travel books and one volume of verse. Associated with the naturalist school, he depicted human lives and social forces in often pessimistic terms. Many of his stories are set during the [[Franco-Prussian War]], describing the futility of war and the innocent civilians caught up in it. He lived at Étretat in [[Normandy]] until the age of thirteen, and in 1871 moved to Paris, where he spent ten years as a clerk in the Navy Department. His first published story, "Boule de Suif" ("The Dumpling", 1880), is often considered his most famous work.

Country in [[South America]]. Officially the Co-operative Republic of Guyana, it borders the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the north, [[Suriname]] to the east, [[Brazil]] to the south and southwest, and [[Venezuela]] to the west. English is its official language, the only one in mainland South America to have that status, and its capital and largest city is Georgetown. Guyana was colonized by the Dutch before coming under British control in the late 18th century, and gained independence in 1966. It became a republic within the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] in 1970. The country hosts part of the Amazon rainforest and has very high biodiversity. In 2017, 41% of the population lived below the poverty line. After oil was discovered in 2015 and commercial drilling began in 2019, its economy grew by 49% in 2020, and in 2025 Guyana was the world's largest per capita oil producer.

Nineteenth monarch of Goguryeo. He took the title Taewang, equivalent to "emperor", placing Goguryeo on equal standing with the imperial dynasties of China. Under him Goguryeo became one of the great powers of [[East Asia]]. In 396 he defeated Baekje, then the most powerful of the [[Three Kingdoms of Korea]], and captured its capital, Wiryeseong, in present-day [[Seoul]]. In 399 he dispatched 50,000 troops to aid Silla, which became a de facto protectorate. His western campaigns defeated the Xianbei of the Later Yan empire and conquered the Liaodong peninsula, and his conquests extended into [[Manchuria]] and [[Inner Mongolia]]. His achievements are recorded on the Gwanggaeto Stele, erected in 414 by his son Jangsu near the supposed site of his tomb in Ji'an, on the China–North Korea border. It is the largest engraved stele in the world.

Series of student-led demonstrations in Gwangju, South Korea, in May 1980. Protesters opposed martial law and the coup by Chun Doo-hwan, which strengthened his power. Citizens formed militias and took control of large sections of the city before soldiers retook it. Scholarship estimates 600 to 2,300 people were killed, compared with the 165 deaths the government claimed. The [[United States]] under the Carter administration gave Chun approval to retake the city. A national day of commemoration for May 18 was established in 1997, and the uprising's document archive was listed on the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2011.

American actress and businesswoman. Paltrow established herself as a leading lady in primarily mid-budget and period films during the 1990s. She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Shakespeare in Love* (1998). Her career was revived by her role as Pepper Potts in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] films. She also received a Primetime Emmy Award for her guest role in *Glee*. She founded and leads the lifestyle company Goop, which has been criticized for promoting [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]]. She hosted *The Goop Lab* for [[Netflix]] in 2020.

Hungarian composer of [[Contemporary classical music|contemporary classical music]]. Born in [[Transylvania]], Romania, he lived in Communist Hungary, which restricted his musical style, until he emigrated to Austria in 1956 and became an Austrian citizen in 1968. After experimenting with [[Electronic music]] in [[Cologne]], he broke through with orchestral works such as *Atmosphères*, which used a technique he later called micropolyphony. From 1973 to 1989 he was professor of composition at the Hochschule für Musik und Theater Hamburg. He is best known to the public through excerpts of his music in film soundtracks, though he wrote no film scores. The sound design of [[Stanley Kubrick]]'s films, particularly *2001: A Space Odyssey*, drew from his work.

Group of sports requiring balance, strength, flexibility, agility, coordination and endurance. Gymnastics evolved from exercises of the [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greeks]], practiced in [[Sparta]] and [[Athens]]. Its name derives from a Greek verb meaning "to train naked", because athletes exercised without clothing. The most common competitive form is [[Artistic gymnastics|artistic gymnastics]]: women compete on floor, vault, uneven bars and balance beam, while men also use rings, pommel horse, parallel bars and horizontal bar. World Gymnastics, formerly the International Gymnastics Federation, governs eight sports, including trampolining, aerobic gymnastics and parkour. In 1811 German educator Friedrich Ludwig Jahn began the German gymnastics movement in Berlin, which led to the invention of several apparatus. Gymnastics first appeared at the 1896 [[Olympic Games]]. Its participants range from young children to competitive athletes at all skill levels.

Clade of woody, perennial seed-producing plants with unenclosed seeds. The name comes from [[Ancient Greek]] words meaning "naked seed". Unlike [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], gymnosperms do not enclose their [[Seed|seeds]] in an ovary; the seeds develop on scales or leaves, often modified into cones. Over 1,000 living species exist. [[Conifer|Conifers]], such as pines and cypresses, are by far the largest group, followed by [[Cycad|cycads]], gnetophytes and [[Ginkgo biloba]], a single living species. Early seed plant characteristics appear in fossil progymnosperms of the late [[Devonian]] period, around 383 million years ago. About 65% of gymnosperms are dioecious, but conifers are almost all monoecious.

Soft [[Sulfate|sulfate]] mineral of calcium sulfate dihydrate (CaSO₄·2H₂O). It is widely mined for use as [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]] and as the main constituent of plaster, drywall and blackboard or sidewalk chalk. It has a [[Mohs scale|Mohs hardness]] of 2 and forms as an evaporite mineral and as a hydration product of anhydrite. Its transparent crystals, called selenite, contain no significant selenium; both names derive from the ancient Greek word for the [[Moon]]. Fine-grained white or lightly tinted alabaster has been used for sculpture by [[Ancient Egypt]], [[Mesopotamia]] and [[Ancient Rome]]. Gypsum is moderately water-soluble and, unlike most salts, becomes less soluble at higher temperatures. Heated, it forms plaster of Paris, which hardens back into gypsum when water is added.

Device for measuring or maintaining orientation and angular velocity. The name derives from [[Ancient Greek]] words meaning "round" and "to look". It consists of a spinning wheel or disc whose axis is free to assume any orientation; owing to conservation of [[Angular momentum|angular momentum]], the axis is unaffected by tilting or rotation of its mounting. Gyroscopes are used in inertial navigation systems, such as in the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] and inside the steel hull of a submerged submarine. Gyrocompasses complement or replace magnetic [[Compass|compasses]] in ships, aircraft and spacecraft, and gyrostabilization steadies bicycles, motorcycles and ships. Microelectromechanical (MEMS) gyroscopes, packaged on microchips, are popular in [[Consumer electronics]] such as [[Smartphone|smartphones]]. Solid-state ring lasers and fiber optic gyroscopes use other operating principles.

American premium television network and service, a subsidiary of Skydance Corporation. Launched on November 8, 1972, it was the first television service transmitted directly to individual cable systems and was the blueprint for the "premium channel", a subscription service without advertising. It began as a regional service in the northern Mid-Atlantic and southern [[New England]], and in September 1975 became the first channel to transmit by satellite nationally. As of September 2018, approximately 35.656 million American households subscribed to a multichannel television provider, the largest subscriber total of any American premium channel. Its content is the centerpiece of HBO Max, a streaming platform.

Proprietary digital interface for transmitting high-quality video and audio between devices. Introduced in 2003, HDMI largely replaced analog formats such as composite video, S-Video and VGA in [[Consumer electronics]]. It is electrically compatible with DVI video signals and carries uncompressed video and digital audio over a single cable, connecting devices such as televisions, monitors, projectors and gaming consoles. Its founders included [[Panasonic]] and [[Sony]], and [[Intel]] contributed the HDCP copy protection system. As of January 2026, nearly 14 billion HDMI-enabled devices had been sold worldwide.

Human [[Virus|retrovirus]] of the [[Genus|genus]] Lentivirus, cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Without treatment, average survival after infection is estimated at 9 to 11 years. HIV is most often sexually transmitted or passed through blood, and from mother to infant during pregnancy, childbirth and breastfeeding. Research shows it is not transmitted during [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]] without a condom when the HIV-positive partner has a consistently undetectable viral load. It infects helper T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells of the [[Immune system]]. As CD4+ T cell numbers fall, the body becomes progressively more susceptible to opportunistic infections, which leads to AIDS. HIV-1 causes most infections globally, while HIV-2 is largely confined to [[West Africa]]. After integration into the host cell's [[DNA]], the virus may remain dormant for up to ten years.

British universal bank and financial services group, headquartered in [[London]]. It traces its origins to a trading house in [[British Hong Kong]], where it was established in 1865 and incorporated in 1866 as the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. The bank financed trade between China, India, the British Empire and Europe, especially [[Opium]]. HSBC has offices in 57 countries and territories, serving around 39 million customers. As of 2025 it ranked 15th in the world in the [[Forbes]] Global 2000. Its shares are listed on the [[New York Stock Exchange]] and the [[London Stock Exchange]].

Two cylindrical-coordinate representations of the RGB color model. Developed in the 1970s for [[Computer graphics|computer graphics]], HSL and HSV are used in color pickers and image editing software. HSL stands for hue, saturation and lightness; HSV stands for hue, saturation and value, also called HSB (brightness). In each cylinder, the angle around the central axis is hue, the distance from the axis is saturation, and the distance along the axis is lightness or value. Because both are transformations of device-dependent RGB, their values describe different colors on different devices. Both are criticized for not adequately separating color attributes and for lacking perceptual uniformity.

Standard markup language for documents designed to be displayed in a [[Web browser]]. HTML elements are delineated by tags written in angle brackets, which define the content and structure of web pages and embed images, objects and interactive forms. Browsers use the tags to interpret content without displaying them. [[Tim Berners-Lee]] specified HTML and wrote browser and server software in late 1990. The first public description, "HTML Tags", appeared in late 1991 and described 18 elements. The World Wide Web Consortium has encouraged the use of [[CSS]] for style rather than presentational HTML since 1997. HTML can also embed [[JavaScript]], which affects page behavior.

Extension of the [[HTTP|Hypertext Transfer Protocol]] using TLS encryption. Traffic is encrypted with [[Transport Layer Security]] (TLS) or, formerly, Secure Sockets Layer (SSL). It protects against man-in-the-middle attacks, eavesdropping and tampering, and its digital certificates allow [[Authentication|authentication]] of the accessed website by a trusted third party. Fully authenticated connections were once expensive and mostly used for payments, but a 2016 campaign by the Electronic Frontier Foundation helped spread the protocol. Since 2018 it has been used more than unencrypted HTTP. HTTPS cannot hide the server's IP address, port or sometimes domain name from eavesdroppers.

Application layer protocol of the [[Internet protocol suite]] for distributed, collaborative hypermedia information systems. HTTP is the foundation of data communication for the [[World Wide Web]]. It is a request–response protocol in the client–server model: a [[Web browser]] or other user agent submits a request, and the server returns a response, optionally containing a resource such as an [[HTML]] document. Resources are located by a [[URL]]. Intermediaries such as [[Proxy server|proxy servers]] and web caches can relay messages or deliver content to reduce response time and network traffic. HTTP/1.0 opened a separate TCP connection for every request, whereas HTTP/1.1 allows a connection to be reused for multiple requests. HTTP/2 added a compressed binary representation of headers and multiplexed streams, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP instead of TCP.

English writer, sometimes called the father of [[Science fiction|science fiction]]. Wells wrote more than forty novels and dozens of short stories, as well as works of social commentary, politics, history and popular science. As a futurist he foresaw aircraft, tanks, space travel, nuclear weapons, satellite television and something resembling the [[World Wide Web]]. His science fiction includes *The Time Machine* (1895), *The Island of Doctor Moreau* (1896), *The Invisible Man* (1897) and *The War of the Worlds* (1898). He trained first in [[Biology]], was an outspoken socialist and, for much of his adult life, a passionate advocate of [[Eugenics|eugenics]], a view he had largely recanted by 1940. He was a diabetic and co-founded the charity The Diabetic Association (Diabetes UK) in 1934. Wells was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature four times.

American con artist and [[Serial killer|serial killer]] active between 1891 and 1894. He committed his most notorious crimes in [[Chicago]] around the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and was known as the Beast of Chicago. Holmes was convicted of murdering Benjamin Pitezel, an accomplice in his cons, and confessed to twenty-seven murders, though his contradictory accounts make the truth difficult to establish. Many details of the so-called "Murder Castle", a building he commissioned in Chicago, are considered exaggerated, and some accounts put his body count as high as 133. He has often been described since the 1990s as the first serial killer in U.S. history.

Ionized region of interstellar hydrogen, typically within a [[Molecular cloud|molecular cloud]] in which stars have formed. The short-lived blue stars it contains emit copious [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light that ionizes the surrounding gas. H II regions range from one to hundreds of light-years across, with densities from a few to about a million particles per cubic centimeter. They may give birth to thousands of stars over several million years, until [[Supernova|supernova]] explosions and stellar winds disperse the remaining gas. The [[Orion Nebula]], the first such object discovered, was observed by Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc in 1610. They are concentrated in the spiral arms of galaxies such as the [[Milky Way]], and extragalactic H II regions, such as NGC 604 in the [[Triangulum Galaxy]], help determine the distances and chemical composition of galaxies.

Swedish multinational fast-fashion [[Retail|retail]] company, headquartered in [[Stockholm]]. Erling Persson founded it in 1947 as Hennes, a women's clothing shop in Västerås. The name became Hennes & Mauritz in 1968, after Persson acquired the hunting apparel retailer Mauritz Widforss and added menswear. H&M is the second-largest international clothing retailer after Inditex, with thousands of stores across 75 markets and over 171,000 employees. Its first store outside Scandinavia opened in [[London]] in 1976, and its first U.S. store opened in [[New York City]] in 2000. In October 2020 it announced plans to close 5% of its worldwide stores because of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].
